title: IF vs IFS
description: See when to use the classic IF function and when to switch to the newer IFS function.
intro: IF is the classic branching function, but nesting multiple IFs can become hard to read. IFS provides a flat list of conditions that is easier to manage.

comparisonTable.functionA: Harder to read with many conditions

comparisonTable.functionB: Use TRUE as the final condition for a default

comparisonTable.functionA: Nested IF limit depends on version

whenToUseA: Use IF for a single condition or when sharing files with users on older Excel versions.
whenToUseB: Use IFS when you have multiple conditions and everyone uses Excel 2019 or later.
verdict: IFS is cleaner for multiple conditions, but IF is still essential for compatibility.

faq.question: Can I use IFS in Excel 2016?
faq.answer: No, IFS requires Excel 2019, Excel 365, or Google Sheets.

faq.question: How do I add a default in IFS?
faq.answer: Add TRUE, "default value" as the final pair.
